papers.title: Prediction-Powered Data Fusion for Treatment Effect Estimation
papers.abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) identify treatment effects without confounding but are often small, whereas observational studies (OBS) are large but may be confounded. Many estimators combining a small RCT with a large OBS have been developed for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the conditional ATE (CATE). However, existing ATE estimators either make assumptions on the OBS or do not borrow enough power from them. The CATE has been studied less than the ATE. Existing CATE methods either assume the OBS are unconfounded, rely on a model of the confounding function, or accept bias in exchange for lower variance. We therefore propose a framework that, without special assumptions on the OBS, fuses the OBS and the RCT by preserving the unbiasedness of RCT-based estimation while borrowing power from the large OBS to boost precision. Applying this principle, we build an ATE estimator, AIPW-Fusion, with closed-form weights and confidence intervals, and two CATE learners, DR-Fusion and R-Fusion. Experiments corroborate our findings.

papers.title: Operationalising Weaker Faithfulness: Recovery, Ambiguity and Computational Limits
papers.abstract: Variables can predict an outcome jointly while each is individually independent of it, causing structure learners to discard informative links. We investigate how to operationalise weaker faithfulness through two approaches: selective protection in an adjacency learner and explicit retention of alternative directed graph explanations. Matched experiments show that changes at both an early candidate-removal stage and later pruning can be necessary. In noisy XOR with a descendant (N = 10,000, 20 matched samples), combining reactivation and protection raises complete parent-pair recovery from 0/20 for either change alone to 20/20, while adding false edges. A confirmation study shows that the family estimator can preserve explanations lost by orienting the protected learner's selected skeleton: in one weaker signal XOR condition (N = 10,000) it retains the entire reference family in 48/50 samples, compared with 0/50 for the skeleton adapter. These gains are conditional. Protection can add only error, weaker effects produce false exclusions, and an ordinary faithful-chain comparison favours the PC learner. Complete nonempty family outputs decline at six/eight variables, and all 400 twelve/twenty-variable searches remain unfinished at the reporting cutoff. Neural controls show engineered retention, while the family estimator returns no accepted graph within its application budget. This operationalisation identifies two deletion stages that must be coordinated in the motivating example and shows when direct family search preserves explanations lost by selecting one skeleton. Finite evidence and computation remain substantial barriers to reliable general inference.

papers.title: Random Jump Forests
papers.abstract: Random jump forests are introduced as a nonparametric tool for estimating conditional cumulative transition rates and occupation probabilities in multi-state models. The main idea is that a single tree partitions the covariate space for all transitions simultaneously, using partially observed trajectories, and with Nelson--Aalen estimators at the terminal nodes. Occupation probabilities are recovered through the product integral without requiring the Markov assumption. Uniform consistency and a functional central limit theorem for the estimators of cumulative rates can be established under the assumption that the covariate vector takes finitely many values, and under suitable splitting conditions. In particular, pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands are available in the Markov case. Simulation studies show a predictive accuracy close to the correctly specified benchmark models and marked improvements when benchmarks are misspecified, with further illustration on four biomedical data sets. In the coverage study, confidence bands attain near-nominal coverage in several settings, with pooling of heterogeneous rates being the main source of possible undercoverage. The method, including prediction assessment and variable importance, is implemented in the R package JumpForests.

papers.title: Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation
papers.abstract: Predictive models trained on observational data often fail to generalise when deployed, especially when the training data is a product of the system being optimised. Recommender systems are a canonical example: they are trained on interaction logs confounded by the deployed policy, past user behaviour, and platform filtering. As a result, the training distribution differs from the candidate distribution scored at serving time, a gap that makes offline metrics unreliable predictors of online performance. We address the distribution shift problem with a method motivated by causal representation learning (CRL). We propose an information-theoretic disentanglement criterion and prove that its optimum excludes confounder-dependent non-causal information from the treatment representation. We derive a tractable variational lower bound making the criterion optimisable from finite observational data. The scope of our method is narrower than that of much of the CRL literature, in that we target better generalisation under distribution shift, not full identification of latent causal factors. This narrower target makes the method practical, requiring only existing confounded logs, applying to any standard supervised model, and adding no inference-time cost. Our headline evaluation is an A/B test with millions of users on Spotify, applied to a production ranker for personalised playlist generation. A CRL variant matched in capacity to the production baseline performed on par offline but delivered substantial online gains in listener engagement. Complementary evidence on a synthetic dataset with known causal structure and a semi-synthetic variant of the public KuaiRand recommendation dataset shows similar in-distribution performance to the baseline but gains under distribution shift. Across all three settings, adding our causal disentanglement objective yields better out-of-distribution generalisation.

papers.title: Learning Bidirectional Causal Interactions with Heteroscedastic Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Estimating contemporaneous bidirectional interactions from observational data is difficult because each outcome is endogenous to the other, while flexible regressions may capture only reduced-form dependence. This paper proposes SEM-DNN, a heteroscedastic neural simultaneous-equation estimator that learns reciprocal structural interactions without external instruments. Identification exploits conditional covariance diagonalization: when structural shocks have zero conditional means, are conditionally uncorrelated given predetermined covariates, and exhibit nonproportional conditional variances, only the true interaction coefficients diagonalize the conditional residual covariance across the feature space. The method jointly approximates nonlinear structural mean functions and feature-dependent variances using a diagonal Gaussian quasi-likelihood that incorporates the simultaneous-system Jacobian. We establish unique identification and positive-definite local curvature of the profiled population criterion and show that, under neural-profile compatibility conditions, the implemented neural criterion inherits this curvature despite nonunique network parameterizations. The coefficients admit a causal interpretation when the structural equations represent autonomous mechanisms that remain invariant under the relevant interventions. Monte Carlo experiments with nonlinear, high-dimensional nuisance functions and non-Gaussian shocks show that SEM-DNN recovers structural effects more reliably than parametric, kernel-based, and separate-equation neural alternatives as information increases, although at greater computational cost. An application to ready-to-eat cereal scanner data illustrates how the method can study contemporaneous price-sales feedback and assess identification strength, residual diagonalization, variance calibration, and optimization sensitivity.

papers.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models
papers.abstract: Simulated maximum likelihood is widely used in latent-variable models where likelihood evaluation requires intractable integrals or probabilities. With a fixed number of simulation draws, its estimating equation is generally biased. We develop Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores (SAUSS), combining score simulation with stochastic gradient descent. The Hajivassiliou--McFadden identity, an instance of Fisher's identity, expresses the likelihood score as the conditional expectation of the complete-data score given the observed data. Exact conditional draws yield an unbiased simulated score for any fixed number of draws. The estimator averages stochastic gradient iterates computed using mini-batches of fixed size regardless of sample size, avoiding repeated full-sample likelihood evaluations. Under local regularity and initialization conditions, we establish asymptotic normality and a functional central limit theorem for the partial-sum process of the iterates under multi-pass sampling from an observed sample. These results support plug-in and random-scaling confidence intervals that remain asymptotically valid when algorithmic uncertainty is non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. We develop multinomial probit as a leading application. In simulations and two applications, SAUSS returns estimates in every reported run, including cases where the simulated maximum likelihood implementation returns none. When both return estimates, SAUSS gives comparable estimates in less time.

papers.title: Parallel Trends as a Spectrum
papers.abstract: Difference-in-differences (DiD) designs are typically used to identify and estimate average causal effects, even though treatment can affect the entire outcome distribution. This has led to a growing interest in distributional DiD methods. However, identifying the full counterfactual distribution requires a parallel trends assumption on the entire distributional dynamics, which can be too strong in practice. We address this problem by introducing a spectrum of identifying restrictions that lie between the average and fully distributional DiD by imposing parallel trends on $L$-moments. This corresponds to a basis expansion of the distributional dynamics. Importantly, each $L$-moment is interpretable as familiar distributional components: location, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, etc. Researchers can pick and choose which features they want to target. For example, the second $L$-moment identifies the Gini mean difference, but does not require imposing mean-level or higher-order parallel trends. Taking a collection of $L$-moments can approximate distributional dynamics under weaker conditions since it leaves untargeted components unrestricted. We develop conditions under which higher-order $L$-moments decay, efficient estimators, and simultaneous inference across growing collections of moments. We demonstrate the benefits of our framework by exploring distributional changes to healthcare spending after the rollout of Medicare Part D.

papers.title: Higher Order Asymptotics of Regression Adjustment Estimators for Causal Inference
papers.abstract: Regression adjustment is widely used to improve the precision of average treatment effect estimates from randomized controlled trials. Interacted regression weakly dominates simple regression in terms of its first-order behavior but, in 50-50 randomized trials, the asymptotic variance of both methods is the same and so relative performance is determined by higher-order behavior. Here, we conduct a higher order analysis to compare simple vs. interacted regression adjustments in the equal-probability case. The relative performance of the methods depends on a number of factors including feature skewness, treatment-effect heterogeneity, heteroskedasticity, and nonlinear misspecification, and can favor either estimator. However, in some practically important settings, including when features are skewed and outlying feature values are associated with higher outcome noise, simple regression can outperform interacted regression by a material amount.

papers.title: The Geometry of Existence and Uniqueness of Maximum Likelihood Estimation in Categorical Response Models
papers.abstract: Nonexistence of the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) under separation is treated as a solved problem for binary logistic regression and as a scattered collection of model-specific results everywhere else. We show that it is one phenomenon with one criterion. In a latent polyhedral categorical response model, every observed outcome corresponds to a polyhedral event in latent variables whose faces shift linearly with the parameter. Random-utility choice, cumulative-link, ranking, multivariate binary and ordinal, sequential, adjacent-category logit, and fixed-score stereotype models belong to this family. The likelihood sees each observed factor only through the columns of its threshold map, the structure vectors. A finite MLE exists if and only if the pooled structure vector set has overlap. Sufficiency requires only continuity, necessity requires only strictly threshold-increasing probabilities, and neither likelihood concavity, exchangeability, nor full design rank is needed. Positive strictly log-concave latent densities and threshold-identifiable polyhedra then yield uniqueness on the estimable span. A single linear program determines whether overlap holds, and convex cone geometry measures the dimension of separation. An application using cumulative-link models for willingness to share health data identifies observations and model terms associated with nonexistence and illustrates how the diagnostics inform model revision and sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: Hierarchical Absorbing Markov Chain Models for Pooling Sparse Combat Sequence Data
papers.abstract: By viewing tactics in no-gi Brazilian jiu-jitsu (NGJJ) as discrete states, we estimate the transition probabilities of tactical progression, while simultaneously exploring the effects of weight categories on these dynamics with a hierarchical absorbing Markov chain model. We further cluster the weight categories and borrow strength using the Ewens-Pitman attraction of Dahl, Day and Tsai. Random partitions allow us to explore the underlying groupings of these weight categories in terms of their transition patterns. The hierarchical structure enables us to obtain an overall mean estimate of the transition probability matrix along with the individual estimates of the weight categories. Through simulations we find that the proposed model is more flexible than hierarchical methods with no partition or fully-pooled alternatives while sacrificing very little efficiency under model misspecification. Applying this method to NGJJ, we found a back-take is the tactic most likely to lead to achieving submission across all weight categories. In addition, we discovered the lightest (66kg) and heaviest (99kg+) weight categories vary significantly from the others in long-term tactical progression.

papers.title: Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference for Extending Trial Findings to Target Populations
papers.abstract: The CODIACS Vanguard randomized trial compared a depression care intervention with usual care for patients with persistent depressive symptoms following acute coronary syndrome. We assess whether its findings can be extended to broader patient populations represented by two cohorts constructed from the All of Us electronic health records. This extension is challenging when treatment effects vary across covariates whose distributions differ between trial and target populations. We develop Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference (PSPI), an interaction-based outcome modeling framework that combines Bayesian additive regression trees for potentially high-dimensional covariates with natural cubic splines of the sampling propensity score. Two variants include a separate spline in the treatment effect component alone or in both the prognostic and treatment effect components. The spline components allow separate regularization of selection-related variation and thus improve potential outcome estimation within the observed range and allow an explicit extrapolation rule beyond their boundary knots under substantial covariate shift. An inverse Gumbel transformation of the sampling propensity score balances compression near zero and the extent of extrapolation. Simulation studies show that spline-based PSPI models outperform competing methods in the settings studied, achieving lower root mean squared errors and near-nominal coverage, particularly under substantial covariate shift. In the application, PSPI estimates larger intervention benefits in both target populations than the unadjusted trial estimate.

papers.title: Bias-aware meta-analysis: beyond fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses
papers.abstract: Meta-analysis aims to synthesize multiple studies to obtain a summary estimate of a population parameter of interest. However, existing meta-analysis methods require strong assumptions that render them not robust to bias and heterogeneity of the studies. In particular, fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes a common parameter across the studies, whereas random-effects meta-analysis models heterogeneity as independent and identically distributed random effects, which still implies a common parameter marginally over the random effects. Due to their limitations, we propose a bias-aware meta-analysis framework that allows for heterogeneous studies with fixed, unknown biases. With no bias, our bias-aware meta-analysis reduces to fixed-effect meta-analysis; with a given bound on the bias, we can still use the fixed-effect meta-analysis point estimator and standard error, but we must inflate the critical value for confidence intervals from the standard normal quantile to a folded normal quantile. We recommend reporting the maximum bias for significance, the maximum value of the bias such that the confidence intervals exclude the null value. We propose a formal model checking procedure and recommend reporting the minimum bias for compatibility, the minimum value of the bias such that the bias-aware meta-analysis model is compatible with the observed data. We discuss the practical implementation of our method and, in particular, the approaches to calibrating the maximum bias for significance. We also compare our method with traditional fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.

papers.title: Honest Inference for Synthetic Controls with Imperfect Fit: Time-Split Validity and the Choice of Anchor
papers.abstract: Synthetic controls are used for one treated unit that lies outside its donors' range, with a pre-treatment window too short for residual-based standard errors to be trusted. We propose inference that separates the periods used to fit the synthetic control from the periods used to assess its error. Weights are fitted on an early block of pre-treatment periods, and the gap on a later block calibrates the bias and the noise. The resulting interval has finite-sample coverage under an explicit restriction on how far the counterfactual may depart from the extrapolated pre-treatment gap, for any fitting rule that uses only the early block. The leading restriction bounds the curvature of the gap and leaves its slope free, and the breakdown curvature at which the interval first includes zero states how much extrapolation a conclusion needs. We show when drift bounds calibrated from donor placebos are valid and how to allow for serial dependence. In simulations, conventional intervals undercover when the treated unit drifts from its donors, while the proposed interval covers whenever its restriction holds and the noise is serially independent. Re-analyses of three classic applications show that some well-known conclusions rest on far stronger extrapolation than others.

papers.title: Direct Simulation of Poisson and Newton Kernel Distributions
papers.abstract: The Poisson kernel-based (PKB) distribution is a flexible and numerically convenient family on the unit sphere used for model-based clustering, uniformity testing, and directional data analysis. Available random variate generators rely on rejection from a von Mises-Fisher, angular central Gaussian, or projected Saw envelope and therefore require a rejection loop, tuning or root-finding, or a univariate setup phase. We show that none is needed. A uniformly random line through the interior point $\rho\mu$ meets the sphere in two points; selecting one with probability proportional to the opposite segment length returns exactly the target density. The sampler is exact, rejection- and tuning-free, uses one uniform direction and one Bernoulli draw, and costs $O(d)$ operations. We place the distribution in the power-Saw family of densities proportional to $\|x-\rho\mu\|^{-\xi}$ and show that, for $d\geq3$, the same construction is exact for one further exponent. This introduces the Newton kernel-based (NKB) distribution, whose normalizing constant is identically one. Across a wide grid of dimensions, concentrations, and sample sizes, the direct sampler is faster than the better of two previously recommended methods in every case, with the largest gains at moderate concentration.

papers.title: Bayesian ACCESS for Understanding Latent Epidemic Trajectories from Publicly Released Suppressed Data: Application to U.S. Opioid-related Overdose Mortality
papers.abstract: Publicly released health statistics play a central role in characterizing temporal trends and identifying structural changes in population health. However, disclosure limitation through suppression of small cell counts, as implemented in systems such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging ONline Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER), produces partially observed count data that complicate statistical inference. These challenges are particularly acute for rare outcomes and subgroup analyses, where suppression is widespread and varies across geographic regions, demographic populations, and time. We propose Bayesian ACCESS (Autoregressive Change-point and Clustering Estimation for Suppressed Count Series), a Bayesian hierarchical framework for inference on latent epidemic trajectories and their structural changes from disclosure-limited health statistics. The proposed model directly represents suppressed count data through a suppression-aware observation model, jointly infers multiple temporal change points and latent trajectories, and borrows information across related geographic and demographic populations while preserving meaningful heterogeneity. We apply Bayesian ACCESS to opioid-related overdose mortality data from CDC WONDER for U.S. states from 1999 to 2024. The analysis identifies distinct subgroup-specific epidemic trajectories and structural changes that would be difficult to characterize using publicly released health statistics without explicitly accounting for data suppression and efficiently borrowing information across subgroups.

papers.title: Score-optimized copula coupling for multivariate ensemble post-processing
papers.abstract: Statistical post-processing can calibrate the individual components of an ensemble forecast but may also distort relationships between forecast dimensions. This paper proposes Score-Optimized Copula Coupling, which rearranges calibrated forecast samples according to an optimized dependence structure to restore potentially lost dependencies. We assess fixed and adaptively updated versions using wind-speed and temperature forecasts. In the variable-specific spatial case studies, all versions significantly outperform the strongest benchmarks, with improvements of 1.08-2.02 percent in energy score and 5.45-7.97 percent in variogram score. A third case study at 24 co-located stations shows that one optimized structure can represent both spatial and inter-variable relationships. The largest energy and variogram score improvements are 3.98 and 3.69 percent for spatial dependence and 1.16 and 1.06 percent for inter-variable dependence; all are statistically significant. Additional calibration terms improve covariance representation but can reduce gains in the other scores.

papers.title: Where the Data End and the Mechanism Begins: Doubly Robust Causal Digital Twins for Treatment Strategies
papers.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used to ask how a patient's health would evolve under alternative treatment strategies. When a twin couples a mechanistic model with learned components and is fitted to observational records, its answer mixes information from the data with assumptions from the mechanism. For sustained strategies that begin at a clinical landmark, we split the counterfactual mean into a part the data support, where patients follow the strategy with probability bounded away from zero, and a part they do not. On the supported part, a cross-fitted sequential doubly robust estimator that uses the twin as its outcome model is consistent whenever the decision model is, so twins that fit equally well but disagree as plug-in estimators agree after correction. On the unsupported part, we characterize the values compatible with the data and with a residual of size at most epsilon around the mechanism. This set is nested in epsilon, reduces to a point when the mechanism is exact and identifiable, and recovers assumption-free bounds as epsilon grows, so the penalty weight of a physics-informed loss becomes a sensitivity parameter. Knowledge constraints on how covariates enter the mechanism shrink the set, and when support grows over time, back-testing gives a data-based lower bound on epsilon. In simulations based on an energy-balance model of weight change under glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy, the correction reduced the spread of estimates across four twins from 0.66 to 0.03 percentage points of weight loss with conservative coverage; on unsupported patients, the exact mechanism was rejected in every replicate, the bounds covered the truth at every residual size not rejected, and a mechanism-free extrapolation was biased by 0.5 points.

papers.title: A Review of Bayesian Surrogate Modeling for High-Dimensional Computer Simulations
papers.abstract: Bayesian surrogate models play a central role in the analysis of computationally expensive physics-based simulators, particularly when uncertainty quantification (UQ) is a primary objective. This review provides a high-level overview of commonly used Bayesian surrogate modeling methods for high-dimensional computer simulations, with emphasis on both methodological foundations and practical applications. We review the advantages of Bayesian surrogates, the challenges posed by high-dimensional outputs, and two broad classes of methods: Gaussian process models, including scalable approximations, and Bayesian basis function regression approaches such as polynomial chaos expansions, Bayesian multivariate adaptive regression splines, Bayesian projection pursuit regression, and Bayesian additive regression trees. We also review strategies for handling high-dimensional simulator outputs, of which dimension-reduction approaches based on low-dimensional output representations are most common. Finally, we highlight key applications of Bayesian surrogate modeling in forward UQ, global sensitivity analysis, and Bayesian model calibration, and demonstrate a practical workflow utilizing these methods in simulated and real data analyses. We conclude by identifying open challenges and future research directions related to method selection, computational scalability, predictive accuracy, and UQ fidelity.

papers.title: Semiparametric inference for a Target Outcome Leveraging Heterogeneous External Summaries of Auxiliary Outcomes
papers.abstract: The integration of external information can substantially improve the efficiency of statistical inference in an internal study, but is often complicated by between-study heterogeneity. Additional challenges arise when external studies examine auxiliary outcomes rather than on the target outcomes and provide only summary statistics. To address these challenges, we propose a semiparametric framework that incorporates external summary statistics into the internal analysis via the generalized method of moments. To accommodate between-study heterogeneity, the external summaries are formulated within a random-effects model centered on the internal parameter estimates and subsequently embedded into the internal estimating equations. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator. While uncertainty from the first-stage estimation vanishes as the number of external studies increases, it remains non-negligible where the number of external studies is moderate. In this setting, we show that a hybrid bootstrap procedure correctly propagates this uncertainty and consistently estimates the asymptotic covariance of the proposed estimator, thereby ensuring valid inference. We further derive theoretical efficiency bounds and demonstrate robust finite-sample performance through simulation studies. In an application to colorectal cancer tumor sequencing data, we show that integrating external information of auxiliary outcomes reveals molecular subtype-specific etiologic associations that would not be detected using the internal data alone.

papers.title: Fitting Dynamic Conditional Densities to Cross-Sectional Returns with Persistent Tail Intensities
papers.abstract: We propose dynamic conditional densities with spline mixtures (DCD-SM) to detect whether the tail intensity of financial returns depends on past information after accounting for volatility and tail-order dynamics. The target is a weighted mixture of the conditional return densities of individual assets in a cross section. Individual distributions may differ, and returns within a date may be dependent. A normalized spline-mixture correction uses score-driven updates to change left and right tail intensities while preserving the reference tail order. We use Wald tests for persistence and assess empirical size, power, and forecast stability in simulations. With fitted references that have dynamic tail order, Wald tests at the nominal five-percent level detect dynamics that affect both tail intensities in the same direction in all 19 US and Japanese equity cross sections, for both raw returns and residuals after principal-component removal with training-fixed loadings. Evidence for dynamics in the imbalance between the two tail intensities is more limited. In the residuals, the correction improves out-of-sample one-percent lower-tail quantile loss relative to these references in 16 of 19 panels, with three significant positive differences at the five-percent level. Forecast gains are most evident in log scores and one-percent quantile losses and are less uniform for five-percent quantile loss.

papers.title: Asymptotic spectral properties and extreme eigenvalues of sample correlation matrices from nonstationary high-dimensional VAR processes
papers.abstract: We study the limiting spectral distribution and extreme eigenvalues of the sample correlation matrix $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ from a high-dimensional vector autoregressive (VAR) processes. Depending on whether roots of the characteristic polynomial of given VAR lie on (nonstationary) or outside (super-nonstationary) the unit circle, $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ presents different types of asymptotic spectral properties. Under both nonstationary and super-nonstationary regimes, the empirical spectral distribution of $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ degenerates in probability to a point mass at zero. The rescaled extreme eigenvalues of $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ are asymptotically equivalent to the eigenvalues of a finite-dimensional symmetric random matrix determined by the characteristic roots. Moreover, under super-nonstationarity, $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ degenerates in probability to a matrix with finite rank.

papers.title: A New Bivariate Excess Wealth Transform Based on Conditional Random Variables
papers.abstract: In this study, we introduce a new Bivariate Excess Wealth Transform (BEWT) to study excess wealth characteristics in bivariate settings. The proposed transform is constructed using conditional quantile functions and their corresponding conditional quantile densities. We establish fundamental properties of the proposed transform and derive some characteristic relationship for some well known bivariate lifetime models. Nonparametric weighted empirical estimation of BEWT has been proposed; theoretical and numerical validation of the method has also been considered in the study, along with a real data analysis based on the Eurosystem Household Finance and Consumption Survey.

papers.title: Partial Identification of Survival Prediction Performance under Dependent Right Censoring
papers.abstract: Survival prediction models are usually evaluated under right censoring by inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW), which assumes independent censoring, an assumption that cannot generally be verified from right-censored data. Leaving the dependence between event and censoring times unrestricted, we derive sharp bounds on the integrated Brier score (IBS) of a fixed model and on IBS differences between models by partial identification. The bounds use the fact that each individual's event time is shared across evaluation times and models, and for more than two models we also derive the sharp upper bound on the difference from the best competitor. A negative upper bound on a difference shows that one model has a smaller IBS than the other under every full-data distribution compatible with the observed data. For a fixed observed-data distribution, we develop estimators, confidence regions, a test of robust strict dominance, and an intersection-union test. In simulations, the confidence regions and pairwise tests performed close to their nominal levels. In three applications, the tests supported the IPCW ranking only for mortgage prepayment data with little censoring, whereas for the other two data sets the observed data alone did not support it.

papers.title: Trend-concordance grey incidence with likelinesses closed-form small-sample inference without elicited prior densities
papers.abstract: Grey incidence analysis ranks the factors of a system from short sequences without assuming a probability model, but the grade it returns has no sampling theory: nothing indicates whether an ordering reflects the system or the few data at hand. This paper reduces trend agreement between two sequences to the signs of their centred increments and analyses the resulting counts with Lovegrove's likelinesses, averages of probabilities over an underlying set of distributions that replace the elicitation of a prior density by a statement of what is possible. The result is a concordance incidence grade with closed-form inference: estimation, the likeliness that one factor outranks another, prediction of future concordance and a baseline for searches over many candidates, with bounded underlying sets encoding partial knowledge. Comparisons whose sign falls below the resolution of the data are treated as indeterminate; discarding them is exact when they carry no information, and otherwise the grade becomes a grey number whose width measures what the data cannot decide. The grade is symmetric in any system and resolves the conflict between the totality and pair-symmetry axioms by moving system dependence into inference. Simulations show that plug-in prediction underestimates variance by a factor of up to 1 + m/n regardless of sample size, and that a fair-coin baseline yields up to 63% spurious patterns in searches, where a correctly bounded set keeps them below 5%. Worked textbook examples and a regularisation benchmark with known truth illustrate the method.

papers.title: Resampling-Based Inference for Incomplete Paired Functional Data
papers.abstract: We consider testing equality of mean functions for paired functional data, where one entire function is missing. To use all available information from the paired and unpaired observations, we propose globalized test statistics that are based on a weighted sum of point-wise paired-$t$ and Welch-$t$-type statistics. By the use of empirical process theory, we derive the asymptotic limit distributions of the resulting test statistics under the null hypothesis and show consistency against fixed alternatives. As they are non-pivotal and contain complex dependencies from the paired and incomplete observations, a permutation and parametric bootstrap procedures is proposed to compute critical values. The work includes a theoretical investigation of the asymptotic behaviour of the two resampling approaches and state regularity conditions under which the corresponding resampling tests are valid. Simulation studies show that the proposed methods provide accurate type I error control and competitive power for most settings under study. An illustrative analysis of functional emission data demonstrates the applicability of the methods.

papers.title: Out-of-sample prediction in SEM: A simulation-based comparison of maximum likelihood and (consistent) partial least squares
papers.abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) is widely used to study relationships among unobserved constructs. Over recent years, the interest in computing predictions with SEM has grown. Different prediction procedures have been proposed for this purpose, including MLpredict, which is based on maximum likelihood (ML) estimation, and PLS(c)predict, which is based on partial least squares (PLS). The out-of-sample predictive performances of these procedures have not yet been compared. In our work, we conduct a comprehensive Monte Carlo study to compare out-of-sample predictions of MLpredict and PLS(c)predict for indicators associated with endogenous constructs, so-called operative predictions. Here, we vary key design factors regarding, for instance, the strengths of structural relations, the training sample size, and the construct types in the data generating processes, which determine the presence or absence of construct misspecification. Across the investigated conditions, MLpredict and PLS(c)predict exhibit similar predictive performance according to two assessment criteria, indicating that neither procedure is uniformly superior for operative prediction. Out-of-sample predictive performance is driven mainly by the strength of the relations between the variables, whereas training sample size and construct misspecification have comparatively little influence on it. An exception is the occasionally inflated prediction error of PLScpredict, which is in line with previous findings for ordinal indicators. Overall, our results suggest that, in the studied setting, fine-grained methodological differences between traditional SEM and PLS-based procedures matter less for out-of-sample predictive performance than properties of the data generating process, such as the coefficient of determination of endogenous constructs.

papers.title: Mixed Engression: Distributional Regression for Multivariate Mixed-Type Responses
papers.abstract: Estimating the conditional distribution of multivariate responses with continuous and binary components requires capturing their dependence, respecting their different supports, and accommodating potentially heavy-tailed continuous outcomes. We propose mixed engression, which fits a continuous generator using energy losses induced by bounded discrepancies and then thresholds its soft binary outputs to produce mixed-response samples. Because the discrepancies are bounded, the population objective remains well defined without response-moment assumptions. However, we show that the full-response energy distance for the complete response vector can tend to zero before thresholding yet remain bounded away from zero afterward as response dimensions grow. A separate energy loss on the entire binary vector captures discrepancies obscured by the full-response comparison and controls the effect of thresholding. The generator is therefore fitted using an augmented energy loss that combines the full-response and binary components. Under compositional smoothness of the structural functions and a uniform threshold-margin condition, we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the final sampler's full-response error for sparse ReLU estimators of models driven by Gaussian or Student-t structural noise, yielding polynomial convergence rates up to logarithmic factors. We also establish consistency when the covariate, response, and noise dimensions grow under suitable conditions. Simulations show improved accuracy relative to the comparison methods under the full-response energy distance, including in heavy-tailed settings. Moderate binary augmentation substantially improves binary-distribution accuracy while largely preserving full-response accuracy.

papers.title: Fr\'echet Kriging for Metric Space-Valued Spatial Data
papers.abstract: Spatial prediction of non-Euclidean data, such as probability distributions, symmetric positive definite matrices, and networks, arises in many modern applications. Such data are naturally modeled as elements of general metric spaces, where classical kriging methods that rely on vector space structure are no longer directly applicable. We introduce Fr\'echet kriging, a general framework for spatial prediction of metric space-valued data. Fr\'echet kriging replaces the weighted average in classical ordinary kriging with a weighted Fr\'echet mean, while the weights are determined by characterizing the spatial dependence structure through a generalized variogram. This construction allows the proposed method to preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space without requiring an embedding into a linear space. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed predictor, including a surrogate optimality property and consistency under variogram misspecification for a fixed working variogram under suitable regularity conditions. Simulation studies for univariate distributions and symmetric positive definite matrices demonstrate favorable predictive performance compared with existing approaches. We further illustrate the practical utility of the proposed framework through applications to exceedance probabilities of daily average temperatures, joint probability densities of daily minimum and maximum temperatures, and inter-industry monetary flow networks.

papers.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a method that first treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with LLM agents as nodes and intermediate textual signals as edges. In NeuroMAS, agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology only determines how information can flow in general, while reinforcement learning training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. Further, we provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular textual computation is more parameter-efficient when tasks admit hierarchical decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves significantly over both inference-time and trained multi-agent baselines. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can be challenging to train from scratch, but become feasible when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned neural multi-agent systems are a promising scaling axis for LLMs.

papers.title: How Much Weak Overlap Can Doubly Robust T-Statistics Handle?
papers.abstract: Propensity scores near zero or one can make standard confidence intervals undercover. Econometric theory has targeted the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) under such weak overlap using nonstandard estimators or intervals. Practice has instead favored fixed thresholding rules that restore asymptotic normality by discarding extreme-propensity units for whom treatment may matter most. I show that standard t-tests for the ATE remain valid even when overlap is so weak that every regular estimator has infinite asymptotic variance. The key is to threshold the usual doubly robust estimator aggressively enough to control bias among unthresholded observations, but mildly enough to control bias from thresholding. I provide sufficient conditions for such thresholds to exist, and propose an adaptive rule of thumb to achieve coverage without knowing the weak overlap degree. In a canonical application, fixed trimming excludes 18% of the sample; the adaptive procedure estimates the resulting bias at five percent of the effect.
